tur15-0: Exercise and Type 2 Diabetes: Blood Sugar, Safe Movement and Home Exercises | İhsan Eren
tur15-1: Exercise in type 2 diabetes: how much and how, what the research shows, precautions against low blood sugar, foot care and six exercises at home.
tur15-3: In type 2 diabetes, regular exercise is one of the most effective ways to lower blood sugar and, together with medicines, to improve long-term control. Because working muscles use sugar from the blood, even short walks after meals help. This guide explains how much and how to exercise, the precautions to take against low blood sugar and six exercises you can do at home.

tur15-12: At least 150 minutes a week of moderate or vigorous aerobic exercise, spread over at least 3 days with no more than 2 days in a row without activity. For people who are fitter, at least 75 minutes a week of vigorous or interval exercise may be enough.
tur15-13: Resistance (strength) exercise on 2–3 non-consecutive days a week.
tur15-14: Over the age of 65, flexibility and balance training 2–3 times a week.
tur15-15: Breaking up long periods of sitting with short bouts of movement at least every 30 minutes.
tur15-16: According to the American College of Sports Medicine’s 2022 consensus statement, regular aerobic exercise reduces both the time blood sugar stays high during the day and how high it is overall. Energy used after meals lowers blood sugar whatever the type or intensity of the exercise. The statement recommends that everyone with diabetes moves regularly, sits less and breaks up long periods of sitting with frequent bouts of movement.
tur15-17: To walk after meals, you can use the walk-after-meals timer.
tur15-18: In a meta-analysis combining 47 randomised controlled trials, structured exercise programmes lasting at least 12 weeks lowered HbA1c by an average of 0.67 points: aerobic exercise by 0.73, resistance exercise by 0.57 and programmes combining the two by 0.51 points. In programmes with more than 150 minutes of exercise a week the fall was 0.89 points, and 0.36 points with less. Advice to “be more active” on its own did not lower HbA1c unless it was given together with dietary advice. The researchers judged the overall quality of the trials to be low.
tur15-19: Exercise does not replace medicines. When you start exercising regularly, the dose of some medicines, especially insulin or tablets such as gliclazide, may need to be reduced; make this decision together with your diabetes team.
tur15-20: The American Diabetes Association recommends reviewing your cardiovascular risk factors before you start exercising. People at higher risk are advised to start with short, light exercise. Untreated advanced eye damage (proliferative retinopathy) can make some types of exercise unsuitable.
tur15-22: Insulin or some tablets such as gliclazide can lower your blood sugar together with exercise. If you check your blood sugar, check it before, during and after exercise; always carry a fast-acting source of sugar with you.
tur15-24: Sweating, shaking, dizziness, hunger, a pounding heart, tingling lips and blurred vision can be signs of low blood sugar. If this happens, stop exercising and take some sugar.
tur15-26: Check your feet every day for cuts, bruises, swelling, sores and calluses; wear well-fitting shoes and clean socks, and do not walk barefoot.
tur15-28: If you use insulin and exercise alone, tell someone where you are going and when you will be back.

tur15-40: No. Exercise helps lower blood sugar and is an important part of treatment, but it does not replace medicines. After you start exercising regularly, the dose of some medicines may need to be reduced; your diabetes team will decide this.

In a study of 41 people with type 2 diabetes, walking for 10 minutes after each main meal was more effective than walking for the same total time once a day. Most important is choosing a time you can keep to regularly.
tur15-43: It is recommended. The American Diabetes Association recommends resistance exercise on 2–3 non-consecutive days a week, and adds flexibility and balance training 2–3 times a week for people over 65. Standing up from a chair, wall push-ups and resistance band exercises are enough to start at home.
tur15-44: Blood sugar can fall even after a single exercise session. The fall in HbA1c, the long-term marker, was shown in studies of programmes lasting at least 12 weeks. You can follow your progress with HbA1c tests at the intervals your doctor recommends.
tur15-45: What should I do if my blood sugar drops during exercise?
tur15-46: Stop straight away and take something that will raise your sugar quickly: a small glass of fruit juice or a sugary drink, or a few glucose tablets. Check again after 10–15 minutes; if it is still below 4 mmol/L (about 72 mg/dL), repeat. Once it has recovered, eat something longer-acting such as a biscuit, a sandwich or your next meal. If low blood sugar happens often, tell your diabetes team.
tur15-47: My feet are numb. Can I exercise?
tur15-48: Yes, but with precautions. The American Diabetes Association recommends checking for nerve damage, balance problems and a history of foot ulcers before you start exercising. Check your feet every day, wear well-fitting shoes and clean socks, and do not walk barefoot. If you have a sore on your foot, talk to your doctor before starting weight-bearing exercise.

tur15-58: Weakness, fatigue, nightmares and anxiety after intensive care: what to expect, what supports recovery, when to seek help and six gentle exercises at home.
tur15-60: Leaving intensive care is not the end of recovery but the beginning. Many people still face weakness, fatigue, loss of appetite, sleep problems, forgetfulness or nightmares for months after going home. These are common and usually ease over time. This guide explains what you can expect, how you can support your recovery and six gentle exercises you can start at home.

tur15-63: Rate of widespread, lasting muscle weakness in people on a ventilator for a long time

tur15-66: What can happen in your body?
tur15-67: Muscle weakness and stiff joints; even simple tasks may feel hard at first.
tur15-68: Fatigue, weight loss, poor appetite and feeling full quickly.
tur15-69: Breathlessness and a lingering cough, especially after pneumonia or COVID-19.
tur15-70: A weak or hoarse voice, changes in taste, hair loss and skin changes.
tur15-71: What can happen to your mood?
tur15-72: Difficulty concentrating and remembering; the days you were sedated may feel “lost”.
tur15-73: Vivid, strange or frightening dreams; sometimes having seen or heard things that were not real.
tur15-74: Anxiety, low mood, feelings of guilt and sleep problems.
tur15-75: In a UK survey answered by 4,943 patients, 3 or 12 months after intensive care 46% of participants had symptoms of anxiety, 40% depression and 22% post-traumatic stress. Two thirds of those with one of these symptoms also had at least one of the others.
tur15-77: The UK’s national guideline (NICE) recommends an early, individually tailored and frequently reviewed rehabilitation programme for every patient at risk after intensive care. According to the guideline, patients should be given information about possible physical and psychological problems, a supported self-directed rehabilitation manual lasting at least 6 weeks after leaving intensive care should be considered, and a face-to-face functional assessment should be carried out 2–3 months after discharge. Referral to a specialist is recommended if recovery is slower than expected or new problems arise.
tur15-78: Keep up the programme your physiotherapy team gave you; take an active part in your own care, such as washing and dressing. Increase your activity a little each day and rest when you are tired.
tur15-79: 2–3 snacks between meals, foods high in energy and protein, and 6–8 glasses of fluid a day.
tur15-81: A regular daily routine, movement, balanced meals and regular sleep. Rest during the day but avoid long daytime naps.
tur15-83: Talking to the people close to you about what you went through and writing your worries in a notebook can also help you sleep.
tur15-85: Gradually, with shorter hours or lighter duties.
tur15-86: Evidence on how exercise affects recovery after intensive care is still limited: a Cochrane review of 6 trials could not reach a firm conclusion because the quality of the evidence was very low. Even so, national guidelines see movement and rehabilitation as a core part of recovery.
tur15-87: Six gentle exercises after intensive care

tur15-91: Lying or sitting, move your ankles up and down. This supports blood flow in the legs and can be done even while you are not very mobile.
tur15-94: Lie or sit with your legs straight. Tighten the muscle at the front of your thigh to press the back of your knee into the bed, hold for 5 seconds and relax.
tur15-95: Use a sturdy chair with armrests. Lean forward and push up with your hands to stand, then sit down with control. Have someone with you; rest when you get tired.

tur15-100: It varies a great deal from person to person. According to a UK hospital’s patient leaflet, full recovery can take 6–12 months and most problems ease within months. In a study following 109 people (median age 45) who had survived severe lung failure, even after 5 years the distance walked in 6 minutes was on average 76% of the expected value; yet 77% of those who had been working had returned to work.
tur15-102: Severe illness, long periods in bed and some treatments can weaken the muscles quickly. According to an American Thoracic Society guideline, about a quarter of people on a ventilator for a long time develop widespread, lasting weakness throughout the body. This weakness can delay coming off the ventilator and prolong the hospital stay. Muscle strength comes back over time with gradually increasing activity and exercise.
tur15-104: Yes, they are common. Memories of the confusion (delirium) experienced in intensive care can be dream-like or nightmarish and can get mixed up with real events. According to an NHS leaflet, vivid dreams and unexpected memories are normal reactions to a traumatic experience and ease over time. If you are still struggling a month after getting home, talk to your doctor.
tur15-105: The evidence is not yet clear. In a Cochrane review of exercise programmes after leaving intensive care, 3 of the 6 trials covering 483 people found results in favour of exercise capacity, but the quality of the evidence was very low and it could not be concluded that exercise works. Even so, the UK’s national guideline (NICE) recommends an individually tailored, regularly reviewed rehabilitation programme for everyone at risk.
tur15-107: Poor appetite, feeling full quickly and changes in taste are common. One NHS leaflet recommends 2–3 snacks between meals, foods high in energy and protein, nutritional supplement drinks if needed and 6–8 glasses of fluid a day. If you find swallowing difficult, you can try softer foods.
tur15-108: My family is struggling too. Is that normal?
tur15-109: Yes. ICUsteps, a UK charity set up for intensive care patients and their relatives, stresses that relatives also carry a significant psychological burden, both after discharge and after a bereavement. Support for your family also helps your own recovery.

tur15-122: Exercise for High Blood Pressure: How Much It Lowers It, Measuring Correctly at Home | İhsan Eren
tur15-123: Exercise for high blood pressure: what the numbers mean, how much each type of exercise lowers blood pressure, measuring correctly at home, salt, when to seek help and six exercises at home.
tur15-125: High blood pressure usually causes no symptoms, so it goes unnoticed unless it is measured. Regular exercise is one of the most effective non-drug ways to lower blood pressure, and in people with high blood pressure its effect may be close to that of some medicines. This guide explains what the numbers mean, how much each type of exercise lowers blood pressure, how to measure correctly at home and six exercises at home.

tur15-132: The European Society of Cardiology’s 2024 guideline divides blood pressure measured in the clinic into three groups:
tur15-136: A single high reading is not a diagnosis; diagnosis usually needs confirmation with home readings or a 24-hour monitor. Everyone over 40 is advised to have their blood pressure checked at least every 5 years.
tur15-137: People over 65 and those with a family history of high blood pressure.
tur15-138: People who are overweight or inactive.
tur15-139: People who eat a salty diet and little fruit and vegetables.
tur15-140: People who smoke, drink a lot of alcohol or do not get enough sleep.
tur15-141: Persistently high blood pressure raises the risk of heart attack, stroke, heart failure, kidney disease and vascular dementia; even a small fall in blood pressure reduces these risks.
tur15-142: How much does exercise lower blood pressure?
tur15-143: In a meta-analysis of 93 randomised controlled trials and 5,223 adults, resting blood pressure fell by an average of 3.5/2.5 mmHg with endurance exercise, 1.8/3.2 with dynamic resistance exercise and 10.9/6.2 with isometric exercise. The effect of endurance exercise was greater in people with high blood pressure (8.3/5.2 mmHg). In an analysis of 24 trials with 1,143 adults with high blood pressure, isometric exercise lowered systolic pressure by 7 and diastolic by 4 mmHg and did not increase the risk of side effects.
tur15-144: In a network meta-analysis combining 391 trials, the effect of endurance and resistance exercise on systolic pressure in people with high blood pressure was not clearly different from that of commonly used blood pressure medicines. However, no trial compared exercise with medicines directly, and there were few exercise trials in people with high blood pressure.
tur15-145: The European Society of Cardiology recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate or 75 minutes of vigorous aerobic exercise a week, plus dynamic or isometric resistance exercise on 2–3 days a week. Exercise may not replace medication; do not stop your medicine without talking to your doctor.
tur15-148: Use a clinically validated device that measures at the upper arm, with a cuff that fits your arm; not wrist or finger devices.
tur15-150: For 30 minutes before measuring, do not eat, and avoid smoking, coffee and exercise; go to the toilet first.

tur15-153: Take two readings 1 minute apart, in the morning (before your medicines) and in the evening. Record every reading as it is, including the high ones.
tur15-154: Look at the average over several days rather than single readings. For diagnosis, measuring for 4–7 days and averaging after discarding the first day is recommended.
tur15-155: To record your readings and calculate your average, you can use the home blood pressure diary.
tur15-156: Six exercises for high blood pressure

tur15-167: Can I stop my medicine if I exercise?
tur15-168: Do not stop it on your own. Exercise lowers blood pressure and may reduce the need for medicine in some people, but your doctor decides about medicines based on your blood pressure readings and overall risk. A UK hospital leaflet also advises not changing medicines based on single readings and talking to a doctor first.
tur15-170: They all help. In a meta-analysis combining 93 trials, endurance exercise lowered blood pressure by an average of 3.5/2.5 mmHg, and by 8.3/5.2 mmHg in people with high blood pressure; the largest fall was with isometric exercise (10.9/6.2 mmHg), but this result was based on few trials. In a newer, larger analysis, isometric exercises such as the wall sit also came out on top. The best exercise is the one you can do regularly.
tur15-171: Will lifting weights raise my blood pressure?
tur15-172: Regular resistance exercise does not raise resting blood pressure; it lowers it. The European Society of Cardiology recommends resistance exercise on 2–3 days a week. Do not hold your breath during exercise and avoid very heavy loads. If your blood pressure is not under control, talk to your doctor first.
tur15-173: Why is my home reading different from the one at the clinic?
tur15-174: In some people, blood pressure is high only at the clinic (the “white coat” effect), while in others it looks normal at the clinic but is high during the day. This is why the European Society of Cardiology recommends out-of-office readings, that is, home or 24-hour monitoring, for diagnosis. A home average below 135/85 (below 145/85 at age 80 and over) is considered normal.
tur15-175: How and when should I measure at home?
tur15-176: For diagnosis, the UK guideline (NICE) recommends taking two readings 1 minute apart, morning and evening, for 4–7 days, discarding the first day’s readings and averaging the rest. Before measuring, rest for 5 minutes, sit with your back supported and legs uncrossed, rest your arm on a table at heart level and do not talk during the measurement.
tur15-177: How much salt should I eat?
tur15-178: The European Society of Cardiology recommends less than 2 grams of sodium a day, that is about 5 grams of salt (one teaspoon). It also recommends increasing potassium intake through fruit and vegetables in people without kidney disease, avoiding alcohol and keeping a healthy weight.

tur15-183: Frequent headaches, blurred vision or chest pain that comes and goes: see your doctor

tur15-248: Why do I take two readings?
tur15-249: The first reading is often a little higher. The UK guideline (NICE) recommends taking two readings 1 minute apart each time. Blood Pressure UK also suggests that if the first reading is clearly higher than the other, you discard it and take another.
tur15-250: Why are the first day’s readings not counted?

For diagnosis, NICE recommends measuring for 4–7 days, discarding the first day’s readings and averaging the rest. This diary calculates the average in the same way.

tur15-253: This is not a diagnosis, but you should share your readings with your doctor. A home average of 135/85 or above (145/85 or above at age 80 and over) suggests high blood pressure. Your doctor makes the diagnosis and decides on treatment by assessing it together with clinic readings. Do not change your medicine based on single readings.

tur15-303: Wear comfortable clothes and walking shoes, and use your medicines and inhalers as usual. Do not do heavy exercise in the 2 hours before the test; if you like, eat something light 1–2 hours beforehand.
tur15-304: Mark two points in a flat, clear corridor. Bring the stick or walking frame you use; have someone with you.
tur15-305: Sit and rest for about 10 minutes before you start.
tur15-306: Press Start and for 6 minutes walk between the two marks, as far as you can at your own pace. Stop and rest if you need to; the time keeps running.
tur15-307: When time is up, stop where you are, add the last partial length and save the result.
tur15-308: Do not do the test if you have had a heart attack in the past month or your chest pain has recently changed.
tur15-309: If your resting pulse is above 120 a minute or your blood pressure above 180/100, talk to your doctor first.
tur15-310: Stop straight away if you have chest pain, intolerable breathlessness, leg cramps, staggering, heavy sweating or turn pale.
tur15-311: If you use oxygen, use it during the test too, as your doctor has advised.
tur15-312: This page is for following your own progress; it does not replace the hospital test monitored with oxygen and pulse readings.
tur15-313: Can I do it at home?
tur15-314: Yes, but use the result to follow your own progress. The international standard recommends a flat corridor of at least 30 metres, and the expected values for age and height were obtained under these conditions. The result can change as the course gets shorter: in one study people walked about 50 metres further on a 30-metre course than on a 10-metre course. Use the same course every time.
tur15-315: Why is it recommended to do it twice?
tur15-316: People usually walk further on their second attempt: in people with lung disease the second test is on average 26 metres longer. So if you are doing it for the first time, you can repeat the test once fully rested and record the better result.
tur15-317: How big a change is meaningful?
tur15-318: In chronic lung disease, the change considered meaningful is about 30 metres (25–33 metres). This figure was mostly calculated from group averages; talk to your doctor or physiotherapist when interpreting your own results.
tur15-319: My distance has dropped. What does it mean?
tur15-320: In a study following 2,112 people with COPD for a year, a fall of 30 metres or more in 6-minute walk distance was linked to a higher risk of death. If your result has dropped clearly or your breathlessness has increased, talk to your doctor; this alone is not a diagnosis.
tur15-321: Can I stop during the test?
tur15-322: Yes. You can slow down, stop and rest, and carry on walking when you feel ready; the time keeps running. The aim is to walk as far as you can in 6 minutes at your own pace; do not run.
tur15-323: To measure your fitness in a small space, see the 2-minute step test; for related guides, see the COPD and exercise in heart failure pages.

tur15-331: Cochrane: exercise reduces depression symptoms, and its effect may be close to that of psychotherapy
tur15-332: In a study published in Neurology on 7 October 2026 by researchers at the University of Cincinnati in the USA, 294 people with mild to moderate Parkinson’s disease were followed for up to 7 years. Participants reported how many hours a week they spent in moderate or vigorous activity, including work, housework and hobbies, and were divided into three groups: up to 4 hours, 4–8 hours and more than 8 hours. On a 30-point thinking test, the yearly decline was 0.478 points in the least active and only 0.007 points in the most active. The movement symptom score (0–132; average at the start 23) worsened by 0.143 points a year in the least active, while in the most active it eased by 0.783 points a year. A similar link was seen when looking at total time, intensity-weighted amount and vigorous activity alone.
tur15-333: This is an observational study: it does not prove that movement slows the disease. Activity was measured by questionnaire, based on what people reported, and the differences between the groups were small; according to the researchers, these small differences may become meaningful over the years. Participants’ thinking skills were good at the start; 98% were white and two thirds were men. According to Healio, intensity considered on its own was not significantly linked to changes in the scores; the researchers think total time may matter more than intensity. A randomised trial called SPARX3, testing the effect of vigorous exercise, is under way. Still, it is one more piece of evidence for how valuable regular movement is in Parkinson’s.
tur15-334: Sources: American Academy of Neurology (EurekAlert), 7 October 2026 · U.S. News, 8 October 2026 · Neurology, 7 October 2026 · Healio, 14 October 2026 · ScienceDaily, 23 October 2026
tur15-335: In the ESPRESSO trial, published in Brain Communications in March 2026 by researchers at the University of Auckland in New Zealand, 64 patients within the first two weeks after a stroke took part; participants were selected with a biomarker that indicates the potential for arm and hand recovery. On top of their usual care, patients had an extra 90 minutes of therapy every weekday for 3 weeks: half had a game-based therapy in which they steered a sea creature such as a dolphin on a screen with arm movements, and the other half had conventional therapy for the same time. Both groups improved markedly during the therapy period; at 3 months there was no difference between them on a test of arm and hand function (ARAT). Despite receiving about three times more therapy, they were also no better than patients at the same centre who had previously received usual care alone.
tur15-336: According to the researchers, arm and hand recovery in the first weeks after a stroke depends largely on the brain’s own spontaneous repair processes; increasing the amount of therapy during this period may not clearly change the outcome. The trial was small, single-centre and exploratory (phase IIa); the usual-care group was made up of patients followed earlier, not at the same time. The finding does not mean that therapy is unnecessary in the early period; larger studies will clarify how much therapy, at what timing and for which patients, makes a difference.
tur15-337: Sources: Brain Communications, March 2026 · Neuroscience News (University of Auckland), 26 March 2026 · University of Auckland, 22 April 2026
tur15-339: An umbrella review published in RMD Open in February 2026 brought together 5 systematic reviews (8,631 participants) and 28 randomised trials (4,360 participants) of exercise therapy for osteoarthritis; 23 of the trials were on knee or hip, 3 on hand and 2 on ankle osteoarthritis. Compared with sham treatment or no treatment, exercise reduced knee pain slightly and briefly; the certainty of the evidence was very low and the effect was even smaller in large, long trials. In the hip the effect was negligible (moderate certainty), and in the hand it was small. Exercise gave similar results to patient education, manual therapy, painkillers, joint injections of steroid or hyaluronic acid, and arthroscopic knee surgery. In individual trials of selected patients, it was less effective in the long term than knee osteotomy and joint replacement.
tur15-340: The authors state that their results do not cancel out the general health benefits of exercise or patients’ preference for it, but question putting exercise forward as the sole first-line treatment for every patient, and recommend shared decision-making. The review prioritised some systematic reviews; head-to-head comparisons were few, patients’ symptom severity varied widely, and in some trials other treatments were given alongside exercise. A network meta-analysis of 217 trials published in The BMJ in late 2025, on the other hand, had reported that aerobic exercise in particular improves pain and function in knee osteoarthritis, with moderate certainty. Exercise is cheap and safe; but it is important to keep expectations realistic and to choose the programme to suit the person.
tur15-341: Sources: RMD Open, February 2026 · BMJ Group, 17 February 2026 · Medical Republic, 19 February 2026 · ScienceDaily, 25 February 2026 · The BMJ, 2025 (types of exercise in knee osteoarthritis)
tur15-342: The Cochrane review updated in January 2026 examined 73 randomised trials with 4,985 people with depression. Compared with no treatment or control conditions, exercise reduced depression symptoms moderately (standardised mean difference −0.67; low certainty); looking only at the 7 most methodologically robust trials, the effect was smaller (−0.46) but remained. Compared with psychotherapy, exercise gave similar results (10 trials, 414 people; moderate certainty); compared with medication, there was also no clear difference (5 trials, 330 people; low certainty). Programmes of moderate intensity with 13–36 sessions in total, and mixed or resistance exercise, seemed somewhat more beneficial than aerobic exercise alone.
tur15-343: Most trials were small and at high risk of bias; long-term data are scarce. Independent experts stress that the conclusion that exercise is similar to psychotherapy and medication rests on few trials, that supervised programmes attract highly motivated volunteers, and that exercise is probably best thought of as an addition to existing treatments. Exercise has few side effects; but always talk to your doctor before changing your treatment or stopping your medicine.
tur15-344: Sources: Cochrane Library, January 2026 · ScienceDaily, 8 January 2026 · Science Media Centre expert reaction, 8 January 2026 · HCPLive · Medicine Today, February 2026

tur15-357: In less severe depression, exercise is one of the recommended options. In moderate and severe depression, therapy and medication are usually recommended, and exercise can be added to them. In research, exercise was also effective when combined with medication or therapy. Don’t stop your medication on your own; talk to your doctor about any change. In the Cochrane review updated in 2026, exercise gave similar results to psychotherapy and medication in the small number of trials that compared them; however, these trials were small and the evidence is limited.
